title: Yōmiyyaati — a whole day
goal: Describe your whole day from getting up to going to bed, and link sentences with connectors that make the story flow.
bekal: describe daily activities in a clear time order
link sentences with بَعْدَين، قَبِل، بَعِد، لَمَّا
ask about other people's routines and compare them

dialogs.title: حَكِي — شُو بْتَعْمُل كِلّ يَوْم؟
dialogs.intro: In language class, the teacher asks Budi to describe his days. Laila chips in a few times.

lines.speaker: اَلْمُدَرِّسَة:
lines.id: Budi, what do you do every day?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: I get up at six and pray.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: بَعْدَين بِسْتَحِمّ وْبِفْطُر. بْحِبّ الْفْطُور كْتِير.
lines.baca: ba‘dēn bistahimm w bifṭur. bhibb el-fṭuur ktiir.
lines.id: Then I shower and have breakfast. I really love breakfast.
lines.literal: after-that I-shower and I-breakfast. I-like the-breakfast much.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: What do you usually have for breakfast?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.baca: laban w zētuun w khubz. w ’ahwe akiid.
lines.id: Yogurt, olives and bread. And coffee, of course.
lines.literal: yogurt and olives and bread. and coffee sure.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: بْرُوح عَ الْجَامْعَة. بِدْرُس مِن تْمَانْيِة لَلْوَحْدِة.
lines.baca: bruuh ‘a el-jaam‘a. bidrus min tmaanye la-el-wahde.
lines.id: I go to campus. I study from eight to one.
lines.literal: I-go to the-campus. I-study from eight until-one.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: At the restaurant downstairs. It's cheap and good.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: لَمَّا بِرْجَع، بِرْتَاح شْوَي بَعْدَين بِدْرُس كَمَان.
lines.baca: lamma birja‘, birtaah shway ba‘dēn bidrus kamaan.
lines.id: When I get home, I rest a bit and then study some more.
lines.literal: when I-return, I-rest a-little after-that I-study too.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: You never go out? Poor you!

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: بْطَلَّع! يَوْم الْخَمِيس بْرُوح عَ السُّوق مَع صْحَابِي.
lines.baca: bṭalla‘! yōm el-khamiis bruuh ‘a es-suu’ ma‘ ṣhaabi.
lines.id: I do go out! On Thursday I go to the market with my friends.
lines.literal: I-go-out! the-Thursday I-go to the-market with friends-my.

lines.speaker: اَلْمُدَرِّسَة:
lines.id: Good. And when do you go to bed?

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: قَبِل مَا أْنَام بِقْرَا شْوَي. حَوَالِي الْحْدَعْش.
lines.baca: ’abl ma anaam bi’ra shway. hawaali el-hda‘sh.
lines.id: Before bed I read a little. Around eleven.
lines.literal: before that I-sleep I-read a-little. around eleven.

notes: **The word بَعْدَين is the most common link in a story.** It means "then" or "after that", and Levantine speakers use it in almost every sentence when telling a story. Master it and your story will flow instead of sounding like a list.

**The word لَمَّا means "when", and the verb after it keeps its b-.** The form is لَمَّا بِرْجَع ("when I get home"). This differs from قَبِل مَا and بَعِد مَا, which take the bare form: قَبِل مَا أْنَام ("before I sleep").

**The word غَدَا means lunch, not tomorrow.** The warning already came up in unit 9 and is repeated here on purpose, because this is the unit where it's used most. The three meals: فْطُور (breakfast), غَدَا (lunch), عَشَا (dinner).
**Don't translate the phrase حَرَام عَلَيْك literally.** It isn't accusing you of sin; it means "poor you" or "come on, don't do that", said jokingly. Used between friends, not with strangers.

**The word صْحَاب means friends, and the singular is صَاحِب.** It's one of the words you'll use most. The feminine singular is صَاحْبِة, and صَاحِبِي can mean "my friend" or "my girlfriend" depending on tone and context — be careful.
**The verb "to get up" is فَاق, and its present form is بْفِيق.** Don't confuse it with قَام, which means "to stand up" or "to rise", even though the two are sometimes used interchangeably.

grammars.title: Linking events
after: The rule is easy to remember: **if the connector ends in مَا, the verb is bare.** The forms قَبِل مَا and بَعِد مَا belong to that group; بَعْدَين and لَمَّا don't.

To link two things or two simple actions, just use وْ *w*: بْفِيق وْبْصَلِّي. Levantine Arabic uses وْ far more often than English uses "and" — repeating it three times in one sentence is perfectly normal.

grammars.title: Daily verbs in eight forms
body: This table uses the verbs فَاق (to get up) and أَكَل (to eat), two verbs whose forms are slightly irregular — which is exactly why they must be learned whole.
after: The verb أَكَل is one of three verbs whose stem starts with a hamza, and all three behave the same way: أَكَل (eat), أَخَد (take) and أَجَا (come, often written إِجَا). The hamza drops and turns into a long vowel: بَاكُل، بَاخُد.
The rest follow the pattern from unit 8 with no surprises. If you're unsure, say the "I" form and attach the right prefix; your ear will fix the vowel by itself.

sections.title: From getting up to going to bed

blocks.text: Notice three verbs formed from the names of meals: فْطُور becomes بِفْطُر · غَدَا becomes بِتْغَدَّى · عَشَا becomes بِتْعَشَّى. Arabic has its own verb for each meal — English only has "to breakfast" and "to dine", and rarely uses them — which makes your sentences shorter.

blocks.title: Watching and phoning: two words that need a complement
items: The word بِتْفَرَّج is always followed by عَ — for example بِتْفَرَّج عَ التِّلِفِزْيُون ("I watch TV"). Without عَ it feels unfinished.
For phoning there are two options: بِتَّصِل بِـ (more formal) and بْحِكِي مَع (more everyday). The sentence بْحِكِي مَع إِمِّي means "I call my mother".
For text messages, people in the Levant just use the English words: بْبَعَت مِسِج *bba‘at misij* or بْبَعَت وَاتْس *bba‘at waats*.

head: Question
Say it
Meaning
rows: what do you do every day?
what time do you get up?
how many hours a day do you work?
what do you have for breakfast?
what do you do on your days off?

blocks.text: The most natural answer almost always starts with a time word, not a verb: عَادَة بْفِيق بَكِّير, not بْفِيق بَكِّير عَادَة. Both are correct, but the first sounds more native.

blocks.title: Three ready-made answers about your day
items: If your days are all the same: كِلّ يَوْم نَفْس الشِّي *kill yōm nafs esh-shi* ("every day's the same").
If you're busy: مَشْغُول كْتِير هَالْأُسْبُوع *mashghuul ktiir hal-usbuu‘* ("I'm really busy this week").
If you're taking it easy: وَلَا شِي، عَم بِرْتَاح *wala shi, ‘am birtaah* ("nothing much, just relaxing").
After breakfast I go to campus.
When I get home, I rest a little.
On Thursday I go out with my friends.

exercises.prompt: Change to the form asked for.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: بْفِيق السَّاعَة سِتِّة. — بَعِد الْفْطُور بْرُوح عَ الْجَامْعَة. — لَمَّا بِرْجَع، بِرْتَاح شْوَي. — قَبِل مَا أْنَام بِقْرَا. — يَوْم الْخَمِيس بْطَلَّع مَع صْحَابِي. — كِلّ يَوْم نَفْس الشِّي.

بْفِيق السَّاعَة سِتِّة. — بِسْتَحِمّ وْبَعْدَين بِفْطُر. — لَمَّا بِرْجَع، بِرْتَاح. — وَين بْتَاكُل الْغَدَا؟ — بْرُوح عَ السُّوق مَع صْحَابِي. — قَبِل مَا أْنَام بِقْرَا.
